text.title: The Boarding House
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: A widow who runs a boarding house in Dublin orchestrates a confrontation between her daughter Polly and Mr. Doran, a lodger, after discovering they have been intimate, demanding marriage as reparation for the loss of her daughter's honour.

e01-mooney-marriage.description: Mrs. Mooney, a butcher's daughter, marries her father's foreman and opens a butcher's shop near Spring Gardens.

e02-husband-decline.description: After his father-in-law's death, Mr. Mooney begins to go to the devil, drinking, plundering the till, and running into debt.

e03-cleaver-incident.description: One night Mr. Mooney goes for his wife with the cleaver and she has to sleep in a neighbour's house.

e04-separation.description: Mrs. Mooney goes to the priest and gets a separation from Mr. Mooney with care of the children. She refuses to give him money, food, or house-room, and he enlists as a sheriff's man.

e05-boarding-house.description: Mrs. Mooney takes what remains of her money out of the butcher business and sets up a boarding house in Hardwicke Street.

e06-young-men-residents.description: The boarding house has a floating population of tourists from Liverpool and the Isle of Man and occasional music-hall artistes, with a resident population of clerks from the city.

e07-jack-mooney-character.description: Jack Mooney, the Madam's son, is a clerk to a commission agent in Fleet Street with a reputation as a hard case. He is fond of soldiers' obscenities, comes home in small hours, tells good stories, and is handy with his fists. On Sunday nights there are reunions where music-hall artistes perform and Sheridan plays waltzes and polkas.

e08-polly-description.description: Polly Mooney, the Madam's daughter, is a slim girl of nineteen with light soft hair and a small full mouth. Her grey-green eyes have a habit of glancing upwards when she speaks, making her look like a little perverse madonna. She sings at the Sunday night reunions.

e09-polly-typist-job.description: Mrs. Mooney first sends Polly to be a typist in a corn-factor's office, but a disreputable sheriff's man (her father) comes every other day asking to speak to his daughter.

e10-polly-housework.description: Mrs. Mooney takes Polly home and sets her to do housework, intending to give her the run of the young men, as young men like to feel there is a young woman nearby.

e11-affair-noticed.description: Mrs. Mooney notices that something is going on between Polly and one of the young men.

e12-mother-watches.description: Mrs. Mooney watches the pair and keeps her own counsel, though people in the house begin to talk of the affair.

e13-polly-strange-manner.description: Polly begins to grow a little strange in her manner and the young man is evidently perturbed.

e14-mother-intervenes.description: At last, when she judges it to be the right moment, Mrs. Mooney intervenes. She deals with moral problems as a cleaver deals with meat and has made up her mind.

e15-sunday-morning-scene.description: It is a bright Sunday morning of early summer, promising heat but with a fresh breeze. All windows of the boarding house are open and lace curtains balloon gently. The belfry of George's Church sends out constant peals and worshippers traverse the little circus before the church.

e16-breakfast-cleared.description: Breakfast is over in the boarding house. The table is covered with plates of egg and bacon remnants. Mrs. Mooney sits in the straw arm-chair and watches the servant Mary remove the breakfast things. She makes Mary collect crusts and broken bread for Tuesday's bread-pudding.

e17-mooney-reflects.description: When the table is cleared and the sugar and butter are locked away, Mrs. Mooney begins to reconstruct the interview she had the night before with Polly. Things were as she suspected: both had been frank in their questions and answers, though somewhat awkward.

e18-clock-check.description: Mrs. Mooney glances at the little gilt clock on the mantelpiece and sees it is seventeen minutes past eleven. She would have lots of time to have the matter out with Mr. Doran and then catch short twelve at Marlborough Street.

e19-mooney-strategy.description: Mrs. Mooney is sure she will win. She has all the weight of social opinion on her side as an outraged mother. Mr. Doran is thirty-four or thirty-five, so youth cannot be his excuse. He has simply taken advantage of Polly's youth and inexperience. The only reparation that can make up for the loss of her daughter's honour is marriage. She counts her cards and sends Mary to tell Mr. Doran she wishes to speak with him. She feels sure she will win because he is a serious young man who would not face publicity, and he has been employed for thirteen years at a Catholic wine-merchant's office.

e20-doran-anxiety.description: Mr. Doran is very anxious this Sunday morning. He has made two attempts to shave but his hand has been so unsteady that he has had to desist. Three days' reddish beard fringes his jaws and every two or three minutes a mist gathers on his glasses so that he has to take them off and polish them.

e21-doran-confession.description: The recollection of his confession of the night before is a cause of acute pain to Mr. Doran. The priest had drawn out every ridiculous detail of the affair and magnified his sin so that he was almost thankful at being afforded a loophole of reparation.

e22-doran-dilemma.description: Mr. Doran considers his situation. The harm is done. What can he do but marry her or run away? He cannot brazen it out. The affair will be talked of and his employer will hear of it. Dublin is a small city where everyone knows everyone else's business. He imagines his employer calling out: 'Send Mr Doran here, please.' All his long years of service would be gone for nothing. As a young man he had sown his wild oats and boasted of free-thinking, but that was passed. He still buys Reynolds's Newspaper weekly but attends to his religious duties. He has money enough to settle down on, but the family would look down on her. Her father is disreputable and her mother's boarding house is getting a certain fame. He suspects he is being had. He could imagine his friends laughing. She is a little vulgar, sometimes saying 'I seen' and 'If I had've known.' But what would grammar matter if he really loved her? He cannot make up his mind whether to like her or despise her. Of course he had done it too. His instinct urges him to remain free.

e23-doran-memories.description: While sitting helplessly on the side of the bed, Polly taps lightly at his door and enters. She tells him she has made a clean breast of it to her mother and that her mother will speak with him that morning. She cries and throws her arms round his neck. Mr. Doran comforts her feebly. He remembers well the first casual caresses her dress, breath, and fingers gave him. Late one night as he was undressing for bed she tapped at his door timidly. She wanted to relight her candle at his for hers had been blown out. It was her bath night. She wore a loose open combing-jacket of printed flannel. Her white instep shone in the opening of her furry slippers and the blood glowed warmly behind her perfumed skin. On nights when he came in very late it was she who warmed up his dinner. He scarcely knew what he was eating, feeling her beside him alone at night in the sleeping house. And her thoughtfulness! If the night was cold or wet or windy there was sure to be a little tumbler of punch ready for him. Perhaps they could be happy together. They used to go upstairs together on tiptoe, each with a candle, and on the third landing exchange reluctant good-nights. They used to kiss. He remembered well her eyes, the touch of her hand and his delirium.

e24-polly-visits-doran.description: Polly visits Mr. Doran in his bedroom and tells him she has confessed to her mother.

e25-doran-comforts-polly.description: Mr. Doran comforts Polly feebly, telling her not to cry, that it will be all right. He feels against his shirt the agitation of her bosom. He reflects that it was not altogether his fault that it had happened.

e26-doran-descends-stairs.description: While sitting with Polly on the side of the bed, Mary comes to the door and says the missus wants to see him in the parlour. He stands up to put on his coat and waistcoat, more helpless than ever. He comforts Polly, saying it will be all right, never fear. He leaves her crying on the bed. Going down the stairs his glasses become so dimmed with moisture that he has to take them off and polish them. He longs to ascend through the roof and fly away to another country, yet a force pushes him downstairs step by step. The implacable faces of his employer and the Madam stare upon his discomfiture.

e27-jack-mooney-encounter.description: On the last flight of stairs Mr. Doran passes Jack Mooney who is coming up from the pantry nursing two bottles of Bass. They salute coldly and the lover's eyes rest for a second or two on Jack's thick bulldog face and thick short arms. When he reaches the foot of the staircase he glances up and sees Jack regarding him from the door of the return-room.

e28-artiste-incident-memory.description: Mr. Doran suddenly remembers the night when one of the music-hall artistes, a little blond Londoner, made a rather free allusion to Polly. The reunion had been almost broken up on account of Jack's violence. Everyone tried to quiet him. The music-hall artiste, a little paler than usual, kept smiling and saying there was no harm meant, but Jack kept shouting that if any fellow tried that sort of game on with his sister he'd bloody well put his teeth down his throat.

e29-polly-cries.description: Polly sits for a little time on the side of the bed, crying.

e30-polly-composes.description: Polly dries her eyes and goes over to the looking-glass. She dips the end of the towel in the water-jug and refreshes her eyes with cool water. She looks at herself in profile and readjusts a hairpin above her ear. Then she goes back to the bed and sits at the foot.

e31-polly-revery.description: Polly regards the pillows for a long time and the sight of them awakens in her mind secret amiable memories. She rests the nape of her neck against the cool iron bed-rail and falls into a revery. There is no longer any perturbation visible on her face.

e32-polly-hopes.description: Polly waits on patiently, almost cheerfully, without alarm. Her memories gradually give place to hopes and visions of the future. Her hopes and visions are so intricate that she no longer sees the white pillows on which her gaze is fixed or remembers that she is waiting for anything.

e33-mother-calls.description: At last Polly hears her mother calling. She starts to her feet and runs to the banisters.

e34-doran-wants-to-speak.description: Mrs. Mooney calls Polly down, saying 'Come down, dear. Mr Doran wants to speak to you.' Polly then remembers what she had been waiting for.

Formalist Reading.name: Formalist Reading
Formalist Reading.description: A formalist interpretation focusing on narrative structure, point of view, temporal manipulation, symbolism, and the formal properties of the text itself. Emphasizes how Joyce's stylistic choices—free indirect discourse, interior monologue, structural parallelism, and symbolic objects—create meaning through form rather than external reference.

theme-parallelism-constraint.name: Parallelism and Constraint
theme-parallelism-constraint.description: The formal structure mirrors the thematic entrapment of characters. Mrs. Mooney's decisive action parallels Mr. Doran's paralysis; both are constrained by social structures that the narrative form itself enacts through its careful symmetries and repetitions.

theme-narrative-perspective.name: Shifting Narrative Perspective
theme-narrative-perspective.description: The narrative moves between omniscient overview, free indirect discourse, and interior monologue, creating a formal instability that mirrors the psychological instability of the characters. The reader's access to consciousness is carefully controlled.

theme-temporal-structure.name: Temporal Manipulation and Simultaneity
theme-temporal-structure.description: The story employs simultaneous action across multiple consciousnesses on the same Sunday morning, creating formal tension between linear time and psychological time. The narrative structure emphasizes duration and delay.

theme-symbolic-objects.name: Symbolic Objects and Material Detail
theme-symbolic-objects.description: Objects function as formal carriers of meaning: the cleaver, the clock, the glasses, the pillows. These items structure the narrative and carry symbolic weight through their repeated appearance and precise description.

sym-cleaver.name: The Cleaver
sym-cleaver.description: A formal symbol of division, violence, and Mrs. Mooney's decisive action. Appears literally in the violent past and metaphorically in her approach to moral problems. Functions as a structural marker of the narrative's violent undercurrents.

currentMeanings.description: Literal instrument of domestic violence and marital breakdown
Metaphorical tool for Mrs. Mooney's moral calculus and decisive action
Symbol of the butcher's trade and economic decline

sym-glasses.name: Mr. Doran's Glasses
sym-glasses.description: A formal symbol of obscured vision and anxiety. The repeated motif of dimming and polishing structures Mr. Doran's interior monologue and creates a rhythmic pattern that formalizes his psychological state.

currentMeanings.description: Literal barrier between Doran and clear perception
Formal device creating rhythmic repetition in narrative
Symbol of respectability and social position under threat

sym-clock.name: The Gilt Clock
sym-clock.description: A formal marker of temporal structure and Mrs. Mooney's calculated timing. The clock functions as a structural device that organizes the narrative's temporal progression and emphasizes the precision of her planning.

currentMeanings.description: Instrument of temporal measurement and control
Symbol of Mrs. Mooney's rational calculation and strategy

sym-pillows.name: The White Pillows
sym-pillows.description: A formal symbol of memory and desire that structures Polly's consciousness. The pillows awaken 'secret amiable memories' and function as a focal point for the narrative's shift from anxiety to hope, creating formal symmetry with Doran's descent.

currentMeanings.description: Literal object in Polly's bedroom space
Formal trigger for interior monologue and memory
Symbol of romantic hope and future possibility

sym-stairs.name: The Boarding House Stairs
sym-stairs.description: A formal symbol of transition and descent. The stairs structure the narrative's spatial organization and create a formal boundary between private consciousness and public confrontation. Doran's descent is a key structural moment.

currentMeanings.description: Literal architectural space in the boarding house
Formal marker of movement between psychological states
Symbol of inevitable descent into confrontation

symrel-cleaver-mooney-action.name: Cleaver as Formal Enactment of Mrs. Mooney's Agency
symrel-cleaver-mooney-action.description: The cleaver appears both literally (in the violent past) and metaphorically (in her moral approach), creating a formal pattern that structures her character as decisive and violent. This symbolic doubling reinforces her agency through formal repetition.
symrel-cleaver-mooney-action.nature: The cleaver formalizes Mrs. Mooney's character through symbolic doubling—past violence predicts present decisiveness. The narrative form enacts this through metaphorical language.
symrel-cleaver-mooney-action.interpretation: The cleaver formalizes Mrs. Mooney's character through symbolic doubling—past violence predicts present decisiveness. The narrative form enacts this through metaphorical language.

symrel-glasses-anxiety.name: Glasses as Formal Expression of Anxiety
symrel-glasses-anxiety.description: The repeated motif of Doran's glasses dimming and being polished creates a rhythmic formal pattern that structures his interior monologue. The symbol becomes a formal device for expressing psychological state through material detail.
symrel-glasses-anxiety.nature: The glasses function as a formal device that creates rhythmic repetition in the narrative, making Doran's anxiety visible through stylistic pattern rather than explicit statement.
symrel-glasses-anxiety.interpretation: The glasses function as a formal device that creates rhythmic repetition in the narrative, making Doran's anxiety visible through stylistic pattern rather than explicit statement.

symrel-clock-structure.name: Clock as Temporal Structuring Device
symrel-clock-structure.description: The clock functions formally to organize narrative time and emphasize Mrs. Mooney's calculated control. It creates a formal marker that divides the narrative into measured segments.
symrel-clock-structure.nature: The clock is both a literal object and a formal device that structures the narrative's temporal progression, making time itself a visible organizing principle.
symrel-clock-structure.interpretation: The clock is both a literal object and a formal device that structures the narrative's temporal progression, making time itself a visible organizing principle.

symrel-pillows-memory.name: Pillows as Formal Trigger for Consciousness
symrel-pillows-memory.description: The pillows function formally to shift Polly's narrative from anxiety to hope, creating a structural parallel to Doran's descent. The symbol organizes the narrative's formal symmetry.
symrel-pillows-memory.nature: The pillows create formal symmetry in the narrative structure—as Doran descends into confrontation, Polly ascends into hope. The symbol makes this structural parallelism visible.
symrel-pillows-memory.interpretation: The pillows create formal symmetry in the narrative structure—as Doran descends into confrontation, Polly ascends into hope. The symbol makes this structural parallelism visible.

symrel-stairs-descent.name: Stairs as Formal Boundary and Transition
symrel-stairs-descent.description: The stairs function as a formal architectural and symbolic boundary that separates private consciousness from public confrontation. The descent structures the narrative's movement toward climax.
symrel-stairs-descent.nature: The stairs create a formal spatial boundary that organizes the narrative's temporal and psychological progression. The descent is both literal and symbolic.
symrel-stairs-descent.interpretation: The stairs create a formal spatial boundary that organizes the narrative's temporal and psychological progression. The descent is both literal and symbolic.

narrator.name: Omniscient Third-Person Narrator with Free Indirect Discourse
narrator.description: The narrator employs a complex formal strategy combining omniscient overview with free indirect discourse and interior monologue. The narrative moves fluidly between Mrs. Mooney's consciousness, Mr. Doran's consciousness, and Polly's consciousness, creating formal instability that mirrors psychological instability. The narrator is reliable in factual reporting but creates ambiguity through perspective shifts.

reader.name: Formalist Reader
reader.description: The reader is positioned to attend to formal properties: narrative structure, point of view, temporal manipulation, symbolic patterns, and stylistic devices. The reader must track the formal parallelism between characters' consciousnesses and recognize how the narrative form itself enacts the themes of constraint and parallelism. The reader is invited to notice how style creates meaning.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: Joyce employs modernist formal techniques including free indirect discourse, interior monologue, temporal simultaneity, and symbolic objects. His formal choices create meaning through structure rather than plot. The narrative form itself becomes a subject of interpretation.

e01-mooney-marriage.note: Establishes the formal backstory and introduces the cleaver as a symbolic object. Creates the narrative foundation for understanding Mrs. Mooney's character and agency.

e02-husband-decline.note: Develops the narrative of decline that structures the story's temporal progression. Introduces the pattern of deterioration that will be repeated in Doran's anxiety.

e03-cleaver-incident.note: Highly significant as the introduction of the cleaver as a formal and symbolic object. This violent moment structures the narrative's understanding of Mrs. Mooney's character and creates the symbolic pattern that will be repeated metaphorically.

e04-separation.note: Establishes Mrs. Mooney's agency and control. The formal structure of her decisive action (going to the priest, getting separation) prefigures her later intervention with Doran.

e05-boarding-house.note: Creates the formal setting that structures the entire narrative. The boarding house is both a literal space and a formal container for the story's action. Establishes the spatial organization of the narrative.

e06-young-men-residents.note: Provides formal context for the boarding house as a space of social interaction. Establishes the floating population that creates the social world in which the affair occurs.

e07-jack-mooney-character.note: Introduces Jack Mooney as a formal parallel to Doran. His protective violence foreshadows the threat that Doran fears. Creates formal symmetry in the narrative's treatment of male characters.

e08-polly-description.note: Highly significant for its formal description of Polly. The detailed physical description and the metaphor of the 'perverse madonna' establish her as a formal symbol. The description structures how the reader understands her character.

e09-polly-typist-job.note: Provides narrative context for Polly's removal from the office. The formal detail of her father's intrusions establishes the family's disreputable status that will become significant in Doran's calculations.

e10-polly-housework.note: Significant as the formal setup for the affair. Mrs. Mooney's calculated placement of Polly in the boarding house creates the formal conditions for the narrative's central conflict.

e11-affair-noticed.note: Highly significant as the revelation that triggers the narrative's central action. The formal structure of Mrs. Mooney's observation creates the narrative's turning point.

e12-mother-watches.note: Significant for establishing Mrs. Mooney's formal strategy of observation and calculation. The narrative's formal technique of showing her consciousness creates the reader's understanding of her agency.

e13-polly-strange-manner.note: Provides formal indication of the affair's psychological effects. The description of Polly's changing manner creates formal symmetry with Doran's later anxiety.

e14-mother-intervenes.note: Maximally significant as the formal turning point. The narrative's description of Mrs. Mooney's intervention using the cleaver metaphor creates the story's central symbolic moment. This event structures the entire second half of the narrative.

e15-sunday-morning-scene.note: Highly significant for its formal establishment of the setting and temporal frame. The detailed description of the Sunday morning creates the formal context for the confrontation. The environmental description structures the narrative's temporal organization.

e16-breakfast-cleared.note: Significant for its formal attention to material detail and domestic routine. The description of breakfast clearing creates the formal context for Mrs. Mooney's reflection and establishes the narrative's attention to domestic space.

e17-mooney-reflects.note: Highly significant for its formal use of free indirect discourse to access Mrs. Mooney's consciousness. The narrative's representation of her reflection creates the reader's understanding of her calculation and agency.

e18-clock-check.note: Highly significant for introducing the clock as a formal structuring device. The precise temporal notation creates the narrative's emphasis on calculated timing and control. The clock becomes a symbol of Mrs. Mooney's agency.

e19-mooney-strategy.note: Maximally significant as the formal exposition of Mrs. Mooney's strategy. The narrative's detailed representation of her reasoning creates the story's central conflict. This event structures the reader's understanding of the confrontation to come.

e20-doran-anxiety.note: Highly significant for introducing the glasses as a formal symbol of anxiety. The narrative's attention to Doran's physical state creates the formal pattern that will structure his interior monologue.

e21-doran-confession.note: Significant for establishing the priest's role in magnifying Doran's sin. The formal representation of his confession creates the narrative's exploration of religious constraint and moral pressure.

e22-doran-dilemma.note: Maximally significant for its formal representation of Doran's interior monologue. This extended passage creates the narrative's formal center—a detailed exploration of consciousness that structures the reader's understanding of his paralysis and constraint.

e23-doran-memories.note: Highly significant for its formal use of memory and sensory detail. The narrative's lyrical representation of Doran's memories creates a formal contrast to his present anxiety. The passage demonstrates Joyce's modernist technique of representing consciousness through sensory impression.

e24-polly-visits-doran.note: Significant for its formal representation of the interaction between Polly and Doran. The narrative's attention to their dialogue and physical proximity creates the formal context for understanding their relationship.

e25-doran-comforts-polly.note: Significant for its formal representation of Doran's ambivalence. The narrative's description of his feeble comfort and his reflection on shared responsibility creates formal complexity in his characterization.

e26-doran-descends-stairs.note: Maximally significant as the formal climax of Doran's narrative arc. The descent down the stairs is both literal and symbolic, creating a formal marker of movement toward confrontation. The narrative's representation of his internal conflict during the descent creates the story's central formal moment.

e27-jack-mooney-encounter.note: Highly significant for its formal introduction of Jack Mooney as a threatening presence. The encounter creates formal tension and foreshadows the threat that Doran fears. The narrative's attention to Jack's physical appearance creates symbolic resonance.

e28-artiste-incident-memory.note: Significant for its formal representation of Doran's memory and anxiety. The recalled incident creates formal context for understanding the social threat that Doran faces. The narrative's representation of Jack's violence foreshadows potential consequences.

e29-polly-cries.note: Significant for establishing Polly's initial emotional state. The formal brevity of this event creates contrast with the extended interior monologues of other characters.

e30-polly-composes.note: Significant for its formal representation of Polly's self-composition. The detailed description of her actions (drying eyes, adjusting hair) creates a formal parallel to Doran's anxiety and establishes her agency through physical action.

e31-polly-revery.note: Highly significant for its formal representation of Polly's consciousness and the introduction of the pillows as a symbolic object. The narrative's shift from anxiety to reverie creates formal symmetry with Doran's descent. The passage demonstrates Joyce's technique of representing consciousness through sensory and emotional impression.

e32-polly-hopes.note: Highly significant for its formal representation of Polly's transformation from anxiety to hope. The narrative's description of her shifting consciousness creates formal contrast to Doran's paralysis. The passage establishes the story's formal symmetry between the two characters.

e33-mother-calls.note: Significant for its formal interruption of Polly's reverie. The mother's call creates the narrative's formal return to external action and marks the transition to the story's conclusion.

e34-doran-wants-to-speak.note: Highly significant as the formal conclusion of the narrative. The mother's announcement that 'Mr Doran wants to speak to you' creates the story's final formal irony—Polly's realization of what she has been waiting for. The narrative's final line creates formal closure while leaving the confrontation itself unresolved.

mrs-mooney.note: Central character whose agency and consciousness structure the narrative. Her formal characterization through the cleaver metaphor and her calculated strategy creates the story's central conflict.

mr-mooney.note: Absent character whose past violence structures Mrs. Mooney's character and creates the formal pattern of decline. His absence is formally significant as a structuring absence.

polly-mooney.note: Central character whose consciousness is formally represented in the final section. Her transformation from anxiety to hope creates formal symmetry with Doran's descent. Her characterization through physical description and interior monologue is formally significant.

mr-doran.note: Central character whose extended interior monologue creates the narrative's formal center. His anxiety and paralysis are formally represented through the glasses motif and the descent down the stairs. His consciousness is the primary focus of the narrative's formal technique.

jack-mooney.note: Secondary character whose formal function is to create threat and foreshadow consequences. His encounter with Doran creates formal tension and establishes the social world in which the affair occurs.

mary.note: Minor character whose formal function is to carry messages and clear breakfast. Her actions structure the domestic space and create formal context for Mrs. Mooney's reflection.

sheridan.note: Minor character mentioned as a musician. Formally significant only as part of the boarding house's social world.

music-hall-artiste.note: Minor character whose formal function is to create the incident that demonstrates Jack's protective violence. The character establishes the social world and creates formal context for understanding the threat Doran fears.

old-mr-leonard.note: Absent character who functions formally as a threat in Doran's imagination. His absence is formally significant as a structuring absence that creates Doran's anxiety.

priest.note: Absent character whose formal function is to represent religious authority and moral constraint. The priest's magnification of sin creates the formal context for understanding Doran's dilemma.

abs-polly-honour.note: Highly significant as the formal absence that structures the narrative's central conflict. The loss of honour is the absent object that Mrs. Mooney uses to justify her intervention. The absence is formally significant as the narrative's central concern.

abs-doran-marriage.note: Maximally significant as the formal demand that structures Doran's paralysis and anxiety. The expected marriage is the absent future that creates the narrative's central tension. The absence of resolution creates the story's formal ambiguity.

abs-doran-freedom.note: Highly significant as the absent desire that structures Doran's interior monologue. His instinct to remain free creates formal tension with the social demands placed upon him. The absence of freedom is formally significant as a structuring absence.

abs-doran-respectability.note: Highly significant as the absent value that Doran fears losing. His respectability is threatened by the scandal, and the fear of its loss structures his anxiety. The absence of security creates formal tension.

abs-polly-future.note: Highly significant as the absent future that Polly imagines. Her hopes and visions create formal contrast to Doran's paralysis. The absent future is formally significant as a structuring absence that creates the narrative's final irony.

abs-mooney-daughters-marriage.note: Maximally significant as the absent goal that structures Mrs. Mooney's agency and intervention. The desired marriage is the absent future that motivates her action. The absence of resolution creates the story's formal ambiguity.

span_3.note: Backstory establishing Mrs. Mooney's character and agency through narrative of decline and decisive action. Formal exposition of the cleaver as symbol.

span_4.note: Description of boarding house life and character introductions. Formal establishment of the social world and Polly's characterization through physical description.

span_5.note: Discovery of the affair and Mrs. Mooney's intervention. Formal turning point where the narrative's central conflict is established. Tension rises as Mrs. Mooney's agency becomes apparent.

span_7.note: Sunday morning scene establishing temporal frame and Mrs. Mooney's strategy. Formal exposition of her calculation and the clock as structuring device. Tension rises as the confrontation approaches.

span_8.note: Mr. Doran's anxiety and interior monologue. Formal center of the narrative where extended consciousness creates maximum tension. The glasses motif and descent down stairs create formal climax.

span_9.note: Polly's reverie and transformation from anxiety to hope. Formal contrast to Doran's descent. The pillows as symbolic object create formal symmetry. Tension decreases as Polly's hope rises, creating ironic formal structure.
